lessons.title: Planning for intake and receiving deliveries
lessons.html:
Planning for intake

Grain intake is the process of receiving grain from producers or transporters into the silo: checking documents, weighing, sampling, grading, deciding where it goes, unloading and recording. At harvest time a busy silo may take hundreds of trucks a day, so intake must be planned and controlled by supervisors at NQF level 3.

Before the season

  • Confirm available bin space per commodity and grade. Plan which bins receive which grades.
  • Check that the weighbridge has a valid verification certificate and that moisture meters and other grading equipment are calibrated.
  • Service intake equipment: pits, conveyors, elevators, dust extraction, pre-cleaners and dryers.
  • Train staff on procedures, grading rules and safety.
  • Agree operating hours and queue management with management, so trucks are not waiting for hours.

Receiving the delivery

  1. Documents: the driver presents a delivery note or consignment note showing producer, commodity and any contract number. Check the producer is registered on the system.
  2. Gross weighing: the loaded truck is weighed. The weighbridge ticket is issued with a unique number.
  3. Sampling: a representative sample is taken by probe at the sampling points set by procedure.
  4. Grading: the grader determines grade, moisture and defects according to the grading regulations for that commodity under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990.
  5. Bin allocation: based on grade, the grain is sent to a specific pit and bin. Wet grain may go to a wet holding bin for drying.
  6. Unloading at the allocated pit.
  7. Tare weighing: the empty truck is weighed and nett mass calculated.

Rejecting deliveries

Some loads must not be accepted: grain with live insects above limits, poisonous seeds, strong foreign smells, chemical contamination, or a commodity the silo does not store. Follow the silo's rules on rejection, explain the reason to the driver with the grading result, and record it.

lessons.title: Controlling the intake flow and quality
lessons.html:
Controlling the intake flow

Routing and segregation

  • Before each load is tipped, confirm the route from pit to bin in the control room: correct conveyors, elevator legs and spouts.
  • Keep commodities, grades and special categories (for example identity-preserved or non-GM contracts) apart.
  • Clean pits and conveyors when changing commodity.
  • Update bin cards or the system after each load so bin contents are always known.

Managing moisture

Grain delivered above the safe storage moisture for that commodity must be dried before long-term storage, or it will heat and spoil. Wet grain is directed to a holding bin and dried. Drying shrinkage is calculated according to the silo's agreed method and shown on the producer's statement.

Managing queues

  • Monitor the number of trucks waiting and the time per truck.
  • Open extra pits or graders at peak times if staff and equipment allow.
  • Keep drivers informed of delays.
  • Separate the queue from the working area so trucks do not block emergency routes.

Safety during intake

  • Traffic control: one-way routes, speed limits, banksmen for reversing, reflective vests.
  • No one enters a trailer while grain is flowing.
  • Lock-out before clearing blocked pits or conveyors.
  • Control dust with extraction and housekeeping. Enforce no smoking and hot-work permits; grain dust is explosive.
  • Fumigated or treated grain is handled only according to the label and the silo's procedure.

Records and reconciliation

At the end of each day, reconcile:

  • Number of weighbridge tickets against loads recorded at grading and at the pits.
  • Total nett mass received per commodity and grade against bin movements.
  • Cancelled or voided tickets, each with a reason and signature.

Errors found the same day are easy to fix. Errors found months later at a stock count are expensive and may lead to disputes with depositors.

Key points

  • Plan bin space, calibration, equipment and staff before the season.
  • Follow the sequence: documents, gross weight, sample, grade, allocate, unload, tare weight.
  • Keep commodities and grades separate and confirm routes before tipping.
  • Divert wet grain for drying and manage queues actively.
  • Reconcile tickets and masses every day.

quiz.question: What is the correct order at intake?

options.text: Gross weigh, sample, grade, allocate, unload, tare weigh

quiz.question: What should happen to grain delivered above safe storage moisture?

options.text: Mix it with dry grain without recording
Send it to a holding bin for drying
Leave it on the truck overnight

quiz.question: Why reconcile tickets and masses every day?

options.text: Because the system deletes old records
Errors found the same day are easier and cheaper to fix

quiz.question: Which law is the basis for grading regulations for grain?
Pits and conveyors should be cleaned when changing commodity.
A weighbridge does not need a valid verification certificate during harvest season.
Which loads may need to be rejected at intake? (select all that apply)

options.text: Grain with a strong foreign smell
Clean, dry grain of the right commodity
